messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
Can nested closed sets with vanishing diameter be shown to meet in a complete space?

If M is complete and the F_n satisfy the stated nesting and diameter conditions, then one may select x_n\in F_n for every n.

Because F_{n+1}\subset F_n and \operatorname{diam}F_n\to0, one has d(x_m,x_n)\le\operatorname{diam}F_n for m\ge n, so the points x_n form a Cauchy sequence.

Where does this Cauchy sequence converge?

Completeness provides x\in M with x_n\to x, and since every tail (x_n)_{n\ge k} lies in the closed set F_k, we have x\in F_k for every k.

Consequently, the intersection \bigcap_nF_n is nonempty.

Does the same condition also force completeness?

If (y_n) is Cauchy and G_n=\overline{\{y_k:k\ge n\}}, then each G_n is nonempty and closed, the G_n are nested, and their diameters tend to 0.

The stated property gives x\in\bigcap_nG_n, and d(x,y_n)\le\operatorname{diam}G_n\to0, so y_n\to x and M is complete.
